title: Latency-Cost Sampler: Proto Memo
body:
Purpose:

This is a lightweight proto memo describing the "latency-cost sampler" experiments we ran to quickly surface directional tradeoffs between model size, quantization, and sampler-style routing. Goal: give product and SRE a compact, readable artifact that can be iterated on and pasted into a one-pager. Not exhaustive — this is a sampling protocol intended to find where deeper sweeps are worth running.

Context / motivation:
- We hear repeatedly from customers: 'we need predictable p95 at low cost for small chat sessions and affordable throughput for embeddings bursts.'
- Current dashboards show aggregate token cost and raw percentiles but make it hard to attribute savings to: quantization, routing to smaller model variant, or batching tweaks.
- This proto tries to isolate those levers in a quick, repeatable runner.

What we tested (matrix summarized):
- Model families: S = 3B-ish, M = 13B-ish, L = 70B-ish (representative open weights from model catalog).
- Quant modes: fp16 baseline, int8 (symmetric), q4_0 (aggressive).
- Router policies: default-latency (route to L if user pinned, else lowest-latency compatible), sampler-proxy (randomized routing based on cheap classifier score -> sends 60% to smaller models on short prompts).
- Batching modes: sessionized-smallbatch (max batch 8, prefer session affinity), opportunistic-largebatch (max batch 64, wait up to 20ms).
- Workloads: short-chat (avg prompt 60 tokens, response 40 tokens), long-generation (prompt 300 tokens, response 600 tokens), embedding-burst (100 concurrent 3-token embedding requests).

Runner notes:
- All runs on the same GPU family (A100-40) isolated machines to avoid cross-noise; driver kernel pinned.
- Warmup: 120s warmup + 300s measurement window.
- 99-run averaging: we repeated each cell 3x and report median-of-runs.

Key numeric snapshot (directional):
- Table: p50 / p95 / p99 latencies (ms) and Cost (USD per 1k output tokens) for short-chat workload, opportunistic-largebatch, sampler-proxy router:

  model | quant | p50 | p95 | p99 | $ /1k toks
  ------------------------------------------------
  S     | fp16  | 45  | 120 | 210 | 0.28
  S     | int8  | 42  | 110 | 195 | 0.22
  S     | q4_0  | 38  | 134 | 240 | 0.18

  M     | fp16  | 90  | 220 | 420 | 0.72
  M     | int8  | 85  | 200 | 380 | 0.58
  M     | q4_0  | 80  | 230 | 460 | 0.46

  L     | fp16  | 210 | 520 | 980 | 2.60
  L     | int8  | 195 | 480 | 900 | 2.10
  L     | q4_0  | 170 | 600 | 1200| 1.72

Interpretation notes: (short-chat)
- Small models give best p50 and p95 for small responses. L model p50/p95 are much higher as expected; cost per 1k tokens for L is >3x M and ~9x S.
- Quantization reduces cost but shifts tail behavior unpredictably: q4_0 shows lower p50 but sometimes higher p95/p99 due to kernel stalls in the current runtime path (we need further profiling).
- Sampler-proxy achieved ~62% routing to S/M depending on classifier threshold, lowering overall blended cost by ~48% for this workload compared to always-L routing while keeping observed p95 within 20% of latency SLA for pinned sessions.

Ascii sparklines (normalized cost per 1k tokens, smaller is better):
- S: |#######-------| (0.18-0.28)
- M: |##########----| (0.46-0.72)
- L: |################| (1.72-2.60)

Tail sensitivity sketch (p99 relative to fp16 baseline):
- S:int8 -> p99 -7% vs fp16; S:q4_0 -> p99 +14% (kernel stalls)
- M:int8 -> p99 -10%; M:q4_0 -> p99 +9%
- L:int8 -> p99 -8%; L:q4_0 -> p99 +22% (observed jitter on context swap)

Embedding-burst notes (100 concurrent requests):
- Our embedding runner shows batching pays huge dividends: average latency per request drops from ~60ms (no batching) to ~12ms (opportunistic-largebatch) for S-class encoders.
- Cost per 1k embeddings equivalent tokens drops by ~6x when batching is effective.
- Router policy had negligible effect for pure embeddings since model variance is smaller.

Examples of micro-behavior we saw in traces (informal):
- q4 kernels occasionally incur 1–3ms GC-like stalls when spilling to CPU memcpy on particular sequence-length alignments (seen in 2/30 runs).
- Opportunistic-largebatch reduces p50 but introduces bimodal p95 when short sessions arrive during an active large batch window — suggests dynamic max-wait heuristics.

Quick recommendations (proto):
1) For short-chat low-latency product tier: favor S/M with int8; avoid q4_0 until we patch the kernel spill case.
2) For premium pinned sessions: route to L fp16 or L int8 depending on fidelity requirements; consider canarying L q4_0 with strict monitoring.
3) For embeddings-heavy customers: tune opportunistic-largebatch aggressively and expose batch-size tunables in the Console; provide a suggested profile for 100-1000 qps bursts.
4) Instrument a 'quant-tail' metric: p99_when_quant_enabled per model variant and per sequence-length bucket; alert if q4_0 p99 exceeds fp16 p99 by >20%.

Action items / next experiments:
- (Ethan) run a deeper sequence-length-aligned sweep to find exact sequence lengths that trigger q4 spills (JIRA-ENG-2983).
- (Maya) build a quick dashboard tile showing blended cost vs p95 for sampler-proxy thresholds (reuse the sampling runner).
- (Zara) prototype dynamic max-wait: do a 0/5/10/20ms sweep for opportunistic-largebatch and measure p95 bimodality.

Open questions / caveats:
- Results are specific to A100-40 kernels and to the particular model weights we used. Different model internals (alibi/rope config, kv cache layout) can change stall patterns.
- Cost numbers are conservative token-cost proxies derived from internal unit-cost model; will need alignment with finance for published numbers.
- Sampler-proxy classifier was cheap (50–90us inference) but we didn't account for classifier infra cost in the blended cost. That is small for short-chat but could matter at scale.

Appendix: quick repeatable runner notes
- repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/inference-samples/tree/sampler-proto
- runner args used: --workload short-chat --duration 300 --warmup 120 --router sampler-proxy --batch-mode opportunistic --quant q4_0 --model family S
- log tags: sampler-proto/2026-03-17/*

Bottom line (one-liner):
- Smart routing + int8 provides the best immediate win for short, latency-sensitive traffic; aggressive q4 delivers cost improvements but increases tail risk in our current runtime — worth pursuing with kernel fixes and a dedicated tail-monitoring metric.

Notes to self: paste this into product one-pager once Ethan's dashboard is up; mark kernel-spill as high-priority.
